But lately, I just... I can’t seem to keep my mind on things the way I used to.

It’s like the words are there, but they just don't register in my brain. And then, because I can't seem to process what I'm looking at, I end up putting off making my calls. It takes me forever to do things that used to be second nature. I just sit there, wasting time, trying to force my brain to work, and it feels like I'm wading through molasses. I really don't know why I can't think straight anymore, but it's making my days so difficult to get through.

Anxious? Oh, well... no, not really. I mean, I suppose everyone worries a little bit, don't they? Especially in my line of work. When you're a loan officer, you're constantly looking at people's finances, seeing how close to the edge some folks are living. I get up, I have my oatmeal, I go to the bank, I come home, I check on the hydrangeas—even if I don't enjoy it like I used to—and I go to bed. There's not much room for surprises, and I suppose that means there's not much room for anxiety either. My retirement is fully funded, my kids are settled... my oldest, Sarah, just got a promotion at her marketing firm, and David is doing very well with his physical therapy practice. How long? Oh, well... it’s been quite a while now. I know exactly when it started, actually. It was a little over two years ago. Yes, two years this past spring. That was when my dear friend, Martha, passed away. We had been friends for... oh, it must have been going on thirty years. There's not much room for surprises, and I suppose that means there's not much room for anxiety either. My retirement is fully funded, my kids are settled... my oldest, Sarah, just got a promotion at her marketing firm, and David is doing very well with his physical therapy practice. So there's nothing there to fret over. It's not a nervous feeling I have, doctor. It's not like my mind is racing with worries. It's just... it's just that heavy, slow feeling. Like walking through mud. But no, I wouldn't say I'm anxious or worried about anything in particular. Just going through the motions, really.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: How long? Oh, well... it’s been quite a while now. I know exactly when it started, actually. We met when our daughters were in the same Girl Scout troop—Brownies, actually, back when they wore those little brown sashes with the badges. Sarah and Martha’s girl, Emily, were thick as thieves, and Martha and I just clicked. We used to do everything together. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Thoughts of... not wanting to be alive? Oh. Oh, my. No. No, doctor, I wouldn't say that at all. I know some people get to that point when they feel so low, but no, that's not me. I mean, I suppose I understand how someone could feel that way if they were in a lot of physical pain, or if they didn't have anyone who cared about them. But I have my children. Sarah and David. And even though they're grown and have their own lives, I could never do something like that to them. I remember when my neighbor, Mr. Henderson, passed away a few years ago—not from anything like that, just a heart attack while he was mowing his lawn—and the look on his daughter's face when she came to clear out his house... it was just devastating. I could never leave my children with that kind of burden, that kind of pain. 

And as for wishing I could just go to sleep and not wake up... well, I do like my sleep. Sometimes it feels like the only time I'm not carrying around this big, heavy sack of rocks, you know? When I finally get into bed and pull the quilt up—it's a quilt Martha and I actually started making together, though I had to finish it by myself—I do feel a sense of relief that the day is over. I just lay there and think, 'Well, you made it through another one.' But I always set my alarm. I set it for 6:15 every single morning, just like I have for the last twenty years. Because I have to get up, have my oatmeal, and go to the bank. People are counting on me to review their loans, to make sure everything is in order. I can't just... not wake up. I have responsibilities. It's just that waking up feels like such a chore now, like I have to put on a heavy winter coat just to walk into the kitchen. But wanting it all to end? No. No, I don't have thoughts like that. I just wish the days didn't feel so awfully long.

Enjoy? Oh... well. I've been trying to think about that myself lately. I really have. Because you'd think there would be something, wouldn't you? Even just a little thing. 

I mentioned my hydrangeas earlier. I have three big bushes of the 'Endless Summer' variety out front, right along the porch railing. Beautiful things, really. Martha and I planted them... oh, gosh, it must have been fifteen years ago now. You have to be so careful with the soil pH if you want that really vibrant blue color. I used to go out there every single morning with my coffee, checking the leaves for spots, making sure the soil was just acidic enough—adding aluminum sulfate, you know, because if you don't, they turn this washed-out pinkish-purple that just looks terribly sad. I used to love that. The science of it, the routine of it. The reward of seeing those big, beautiful blooms when summer finally hit. 

But now? I still go out there. I still water them. I still deadhead the spent blooms with my pruning shears because if you don't, the bushes just look unkempt, and I can't stand an unkempt yard. The neighbors notice, you know. Mrs. Gable across the street certainly notices everything, she's always peeking out her front blinds. But... the joy of it? The pleasure? It’s just completely gone. It feels exactly like reviewing a loan application for someone who forgot to attach their W-2s. It’s just a task. A chore I have to check off my list before I can go back inside.

And it's the same with my Sunday crosswords. I used to do the big puzzle in the paper, in pen, if you can believe it. Every Sunday morning, sitting at the kitchen island with a cup of Earl Grey tea. I’d spend hours on it, and I felt so accomplished when I filled in that last little square. But the last few months... I look at the grid and I just... I don't care. I don't care what a five-letter word for 'a type of heron' is. I just fold the paper right back up and put it straight into the recycling bin. I don't even make the tea anymore, just pour a glass of tap water. 

So, no, doctor. I really can't think of anything that gives me that spark of pleasure anymore. Everything is just... well, it's just maintenance. Just keeping the wheels turning so the cart doesn't tip over, I suppose.

Small pleasures... looking forward to things... oh, doctor, I really wish I could say yes. I sit here and I try to search my mind for just one thing, but... well, no. Not really. 

I used to, of course. I used to look forward to Saturday mornings so much. There’s a little bakery down on Main Street—Olsen’s, they’ve been there since Sarah and David were just in elementary school. I used to go every Saturday at exactly 7:30 in the morning to get a half-dozen of their almond croissants. They make them with this wonderful almond paste that isn't too sweet, just perfect. Martha and I would sit on the back patio with our coffee and those croissants, and it was just... it was the highlight of my week. Just a small, simple thing, but I would think about it on Thursday and Friday, just anticipating it.

But now? I haven't been to Olsen's in... oh, goodness, it must be over a year. The thought of getting in the car, driving down there, finding parking on Main Street which is always a nightmare on weekends anyway, and then making small talk with Mrs. Olsen... she always asks about the kids, which is lovely of her, it really is, but it just takes so much energy to smile and give all the updates and pretend everything is just fine and dandy. It just feels so exhausting even thinking about it. So I stopped going. I just eat my plain oatmeal on Saturdays now, same as every other day.

And you'd think maybe I'd look forward to the evenings, right? After being at the bank all day, dealing with people's credit scores and debt consolidations and all the endless paperwork—you'd think I'd be eager to just come home and take my shoes off. But coming home just means walking into an empty house where the quiet is just... well, it's almost deafening. So I don't look forward to that either. 

I just exist through the day, really. I wake up, I go to the bank, I come home, I go to sleep. I can't really pinpoint a single thing, big or small, that gives me that little flutter of anticipation anymore. It's just a long stretch of gray, if that makes sense. Just... flat.

Well, doctor, I suppose it’s really just like I was saying a moment ago about looking forward to things... it’s the exact same story when it comes to actually enjoying them in the moment. I don't... I don't find pleasure in them anymore. Any of them, really. 

Take my garden, for instance. I mentioned my flower beds earlier. So I drag myself out there, I kneel down on my little green foam pad, I take my pruning shears, and I clip away the dead blooms. But while I'm doing it, I just feel... empty. And it’s like that with everything. Even sitting down with a cup of tea. I have this special chamomile and lavender blend I order from a catalog in the mail, it comes in these delicate little silk pyramid bags. It’s like all the color and flavor has just been drained out of my life. I do things because they need doing, or because I’m supposed to, but the actual enjoyment? That spark of happiness while I'm doing it? It’s just... it's just completely gone.

Weight? Oh, no, I don't believe so. I mean, I haven't noticed my clothes fitting any differently, anyway. But it just... it never did. It’s been over two years of just this flat, gray, trudging feeling. Every single day since we buried her. I mean, I suppose I understand how someone could feel that way if they were in a lot of physical pain, or if they didn't have anyone who cared about them. But I have my children. Sarah and David. I remember when my neighbor, Mr. Henderson, passed away a few years ago—not from anything like that, just a heart attack while he was mowing his lawn—and the look on his daughter's face when she came to clear out his house... it was just devastating. I just lay there and think, 'Well, you made it through another one.' But I always set my alarm. I set it for 6:15 every single morning, just like I have for the last twenty years. Everyone tells you grief takes time, that you just have to ride it out, let the waves wash over you. And I did. I waited for the waves to recede, for the color to come back into things. But it just... it never did. It’s been over two years of just this flat, gray, trudging feeling. Every single day since we buried her. I keep thinking one morning I'll wake up and feel like myself again, like the woman who used to argue with Martha over fertilizer brands, but... well, it’s been two years, and I’m still just walking through the mud.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just go to sleep and not wake up?\n\nPatient: Thoughts of... not wanting to be alive? I just lay there and think, 'Well, you made it through another one.' But I always set my alarm. I set it for 6:15 every single morning, just like I have for the last twenty years. Pleasure? Oh, my. Well... I really have to stop and think about that. You would think there would be something, wouldn't you? Just one little thing. I mean, I try. Just... flat.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities, no matter how small, that you still find yourself looking forward to?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying with the bakery... I really wish I could give you a different answer, I truly do. Because it sounds so awful to sit here and say no, doesn't it? But... no. There really isn't anything at all. \n\nI try to think about my work, you know, because being a loan officer, you get to be part of these big moments in people's lives. I used to look forward to closing days so much. Oh, closing days were just wonderful. I’d have this special folder I’d put their paperwork in—a nice, heavy cardstock one, a deep burgundy color, not those flimsy cheap manila ones the bank orders in bulk. I’d buy them myself at the office supply store just for my first-time homebuyers. I'd look forward to seeing their faces light up when everything was finalized, knowing I helped them get their starter home. \n\nBut now? I see a closing on my calendar and I just feel... tired. It’s just more signatures to witness, more copies to make, more files to scan into the system. It doesn't matter if it's a big thing like a closing day, or a tiny thing like... well, like watching Jeopardy. I used to watch Jeopardy every single night at 7:00 PM sharp. I'd rush through doing the dinner dishes just to make sure I was sitting in my armchair before the music started. I looked forward to that half-hour so much, trying to guess the answers before the contestants. But lately, the TV just stays off. The noise of it just feels grating, somehow, so I just sit in the quiet. \n\nSo, I search and search my mind, doctor, because I want to be helpful, I want to say 'yes, this one little thing gives me something to look forward to,' but I'd just be making it up. There's just... nothing. Just the same flat feeling, day after day.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or enjoy doing?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I suppose it’s really just like I was saying a moment ago about looking forward to things... it’s the exact same story when it comes to actually enjoying them in the moment. I don't... I don't find pleasure in them anymore. Any of them, really. \n\nTake my garden, for instance. I mentioned my flower beds earlier. I have these wonderful hydrangeas along the south side of the house—they've been there for years, and I always took such meticulous care of them. I used to get so much joy out of tinkering with the soil acidity, you know, adding just the right amount of aluminum sulfate so the blooms would turn this brilliant, deep blue instead of pink. I’d spend hours out there on my weekends, and when a neighbor would walk by and compliment them, I’d just beam. I felt so much pride and genuine happiness just getting my hands dirty. \n\nBut now? I still go out there, because if I don't, the weeds will take over and the bushes will look terrible, and I can't stand the thought of the neighbors whispering about the state of my yard. So I drag myself out there, I kneel down on my little green foam pad, I take my pruning shears, and I clip away the dead blooms. But while I'm doing it, I just feel... empty. There’s no satisfaction when I step back to look at a neatly pruned row. It’s just another chore that I forced myself to get through. \n\nAnd it’s like that with everything. Even sitting down with a cup of tea. I have this special chamomile and lavender blend I order from a catalog in the mail, it comes in these delicate little silk pyramid bags. Making a cup of that used to be my absolute favorite way to unwind on a Sunday afternoon. Now, I brew it, I sit in my chair, I take a sip, and it just tastes like hot water. It’s like all the color and flavor has just been drained out of my life. I do things because they need doing, or because I’m supposed to, but the actual enjoyment? That spark of happiness while I'm doing it? It’s just... it's just completely gone.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?\n\nPatient: Weight? Oh, no, I don't believe so. I mean, I haven't noticed my clothes fitting any differently, anyway. I have these tailored slacks I wear to the bank—navy blue and charcoal gray, mostly, because you really have to look put-together and professional when you're sitting across a desk discussing people's mortgages and financial futures. I bought them at Macy's, oh, it must be three or four years ago now, during one of their big semi-annual sales, and they still fit exactly the same around the waist. \n\nI know sometimes when people feel... well, the way I've been feeling, they just stop eating entirely and just waste away. Usually just turkey on whole wheat, very plain, no mayonnaise because it spoils if someone leaves the breakroom fridge open—which happens far more often than you'd think with the new tellers we've hired recently, they just don't pay attention. And then for dinner, well, I just don't have the energy to cook a real meal anymore. I used to make proper dinners, pot roasts and casseroles and things, but now I just microwave a frozen dinner, usually one of those low-sodium ones, and eat it in my armchair in the quiet. \n\nSo I'm still taking in food, just out of sheer habit, really. I haven't made some grand, terrible mistake in my life that I'm sitting around punishing myself for. I just wake up, go to work, eat my plain turkey sandwich, and come home to a quiet house. There's no guilt there. There's really no strong feeling there at all, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel guilty about anything in particular.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have had at least two weeks where you felt this heavy, flat feeling nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Two weeks? It’s like all the color and flavor has just been drained out of my life. I do things because they need doing, or because I’m supposed to, but the actual enjoyment? That spark of happiness while I'm doing it? It’s just... it's just completely gone.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?\n\nPatient: Weight? Oh, no, I don't believe so. I mean, I haven't noticed my clothes fitting any differently, anyway. I have these tailored slacks I wear to the bank—navy blue and charcoal gray, mostly, because you really have to look put-together and professional when you're sitting across a desk discussing people's mortgages and financial futures. I bought them at Macy's, oh, it must be three or four years ago now, during one of their big semi-annual sales, and they still fit exactly the same around the waist. \n\nI know sometimes when people feel... well, the way I've been feeling, they just stop eating entirely and just waste away. But that hasn't happened to me. Like I mentioned earlier with my plain oatmeal on Saturdays, I still eat. I don't enjoy it, of course, it's just like the tea, everything just tastes like cardboard these days. But I know I have to put something in my stomach to get through the workday. \n\nSo I'll have my oatmeal in the morning, and then for lunch at the bank, I just bring a sandwich. Usually just turkey on whole wheat, very plain, no mayonnaise because it spoils if someone leaves the breakroom fridge open—which happens far more often than you'd think with the new tellers we've hired recently, they just don't pay attention. And then for dinner, well, I just don't have the energy to cook a real meal anymore. I used to make proper dinners, pot roasts and casseroles and things, but now I just microwave a frozen dinner, usually one of those low-sodium ones, and eat it in my armchair in the quiet. \n\nSo I'm still taking in food, just out of sheer habit, really. I actually stepped on the scale in my master bathroom just last week—it's one of those old analog ones, not the digital kind where the battery is always dying right when you need it—and the needle was hovering exactly where it always does. So no, doctor, no weight loss to speak of. I'm just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty or blame yourself for anything in particular?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Blame myself? Well... no, I don't believe so. I mean, I've sat in my armchair in the evenings and really searched my mind about it, because you hear about people feeling like they've done something wrong, or feeling like they're a terrible burden to everyone around them. But I don't have that. I've always been a very responsible, by-the-book sort of person. Ever since I got my associate's degree all those years ago and started working my way up, I've just done what you're supposed to do. I pay my bills on time, I keep my house tidy, I don't cause trouble for anyone. \n\nI know at the bank, some of the younger loan officers—the ones who haven't been doing this very long—they get just eaten up with guilt when they have to decline a mortgage application. I haven't made some grand, terrible mistake in my life that I'm sitting around punishing myself for. I just wake up, go to work, eat my plain turkey sandwich, and come home to a quiet house. There's no guilt there. There's really no strong feeling there at all, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel guilty about anything in particular.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have had at least two weeks where you felt this heavy, flat feeling nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Two weeks? Oh, doctor, if it had only been two weeks, I don't think I would have even bothered making an appointment. It’s... well, most days, really. Nearly every single day for I don't even know how long now. \n\nThere is just this... this dull heaviness sitting with me from the moment I wake up. We meet in this drafty little multi-purpose room in the back, but I always used to love it. It used to really lift me up, being part of the community, balancing their little ledger, talking with the other board members about the heritage day parade. \n\nBut now? Whether I'm at the community center or out in my yard with the pruning shears, places that used to bring me such genuine peace... I just feel that same heavy, flat emptiness. You can't just sit there looking miserable and bringing everyone else down while they're trying to pass a motion about a bake sale. You have to maintain appearances, especially when everyone knows you from the bank. It is like the color is still there in the world, but the feeling of the color is completely gone. \n\nI even tried watching that baking program everyone at the bank is always raving about in the breakroom. But it was just noise on the screen. I ended up turning the television off and just sitting in the quiet. So, to answer your question, doctor... no. I really can not think of a single thing right now that gives me that sense of pleasure anymore. It is all just things I do to pass the time until the day is over.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in the intensity of this heavy feeling over the past two years?\n\nPatient: Two years... well, doctor, it is actually quite perceptive of you to say two years specifically. Weight? Oh... no, no I haven't. You know, you hear about people wasting away when they go through a hard time, but that hasn't happened to me at all.

But that hasn't happened to me. Like I mentioned earlier with my plain oatmeal on Saturdays, I still eat. I don't enjoy it, of course, it's just like the tea, everything just tastes like cardboard these days. But I know I have to put something in my stomach to get through the workday. \n\nSo I'll have my oatmeal in the morning, and then for lunch at the bank, I just bring a sandwich. Usually just turkey on whole wheat, very plain, no mayonnaise because it spoils if someone leaves the breakroom fridge open—which happens far more often than you'd think with the new tellers we've hired recently, they just don't pay attention. And then for dinner, well, I just don't have the energy to cook a real meal anymore. I used to make proper dinners, pot roasts and casseroles and things, but now I just microwave a frozen dinner, usually one of those low-sodium ones, and eat it in my armchair in the quiet. \n\nSo I'm still taking in food, just out of sheer habit, really. I actually stepped on the scale in my master bathroom just last week—it's one of those old analog ones, not the digital kind where the battery is always dying right when you need it—and the needle was hovering exactly where it always does. So no, doctor, no weight loss to speak of. I'm just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty or blame yourself for anything in particular?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Blame myself? Well... no, I don't believe so. I mean, I've sat in my armchair in the evenings and really searched my mind about it, because you hear about people feeling like they've done something wrong, or feeling like they're a terrible burden to everyone around them. But I don't have that. I've always been a very responsible, by-the-book sort of person. Ever since I got my associate's degree all those years ago and started working my way up, I've just done what you're supposed to do. I pay my bills on time, I keep my house tidy, I don't cause trouble for anyone. \n\nI know at the bank, some of the younger loan officers—the ones who haven't been doing this very long—they get just eaten up with guilt when they have to decline a mortgage application. They'll come into my office, usually right before lunch, wringing their hands and saying, 'Oh, I feel so terrible, they were such a nice young couple, I feel like I'm ruining their lives.' And I always tell them, 'The numbers are the numbers. You didn't create their credit history.' I used to feel a little twinge of sympathy for the applicants, of course, but I never felt guilty, because I was just doing my job properly. \n\nAnd it's the same with how I'm feeling now. I don't blame myself for this... this emptiness. I didn't ask for it, and I certainly didn't do anything to bring it on. I haven't made some grand, terrible mistake in my life that I'm sitting around punishing myself for. I just wake up, go to work, eat my plain turkey sandwich, and come home to a quiet house. There's no guilt there. There's really no strong feeling there at all, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel guilty about anything in particular.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have had at least two weeks where you felt this heavy, flat feeling nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Two weeks? Oh, doctor, if it had only been two weeks, I don't think I would have even bothered making an appointment. I would have just assumed I was coming down with a cold or was overtired from the end-of-the-month reconciliations at the bank. No, it's been much, much longer than that. It’s... well, most days, really. Nearly every single day for I don't even know how long now. \n\nThere is just this... this dull heaviness sitting with me from the moment I wake up. It’s like wearing one of those lead aprons they put on you at the dentist's office for an X-ray, except I'm carrying it around from the minute I put my slippers on in the morning. And it doesn't matter where I go or what I do, it just follows me. \n\nEven when I try to do the things I’m supposed to do, the things that used to make me feel like myself. Like I mentioned my garden earlier, or when I go down to the community center. I volunteer there on Thursday evenings with the local historical society—I’m the treasurer, naturally, given my background with loans and financing, and I've been doing that for at least eight or nine years now. We meet in this drafty little multi-purpose room in the back, but I always used to love it. It used to really lift me up, being part of the community, balancing their little ledger, talking with the other board members about the heritage day parade. \n\nBut now? Whether I'm at the community center or out in my yard with the pruning shears, places that used to bring me such genuine peace... I just feel that same heavy, flat emptiness. I sit there at the folding tables during the meetings, and I realize I’m just going through the motions. I have this pleasant little smile pasted on my face because, well, you have to, don't you? You can't just sit there looking miserable and bringing everyone else down while they're trying to pass a motion about a bake sale. You have to maintain appearances, especially when everyone knows you from the bank. So I sit there, and I smile, and I nod, but underneath it all, that dull heaviness is just sitting right there with me. So yes, to answer your question, it's been every day for far, far longer than just two weeks.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any activity, no matter how small, that you still find gives you some sense of pleasure?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? Oh, my. Well... I really have to stop and think about that. You would think there would be something, wouldn't you? Just one little thing. I mean, I try. I really do try to find little moments, because I know that is what people always suggest, finding joy in the small everyday things. But... no. Honestly, no. \n\nI was just thinking about this on Sunday. I have this bird feeder out in the backyard. It is one of those nice cedar ones, shaped like a little gazebo. I bought it at the local hardware store—not the big chain stores, but the little family-owned place on Main Street, because I believe in supporting local businesses, especially since I know firsthand from the bank how hard it is for them to secure commercial loans these days. Anyway, I used to get such a kick out of watching the cardinals and the blue jays come to the feeder. I buy the special black oil sunflower seeds, the expensive kind that does not have all that cheap milo filler that the birds just kick out onto the grass anyway. I used to sit by the kitchen window with my morning tea and just feel so... content, I suppose, watching them flutter around. \n\nBut this past Sunday, I was sitting right there in the same chair, at the same window. The feeder was full, there were three beautiful bright red cardinals right there, just picture-perfect against the green leaves. And I just looked at them, and... nothing. Not a single spark of joy. I just stared at them and thought about how I was going to have to go out and sweep the empty seed husks off the patio eventually. It is like the color is still there in the world, but the feeling of the color is completely gone. \n\nI even tried watching that baking program everyone at the bank is always raving about in the breakroom. They say it is so soothing and delightful. I sat in my armchair and watched three whole episodes back-to-back, just waiting to feel a little bit of amusement, or even just a mild interest in whether their cakes were going to turn out right. But it was just noise on the screen. I ended up turning the television off and just sitting in the quiet. So, to answer your question, doctor... no. I really can not think of a single thing right now that gives me that sense of pleasure anymore. It is all just things I do to pass the time until the day is over.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in the intensity of this heavy feeling over the past two years?\n\nPatient: Two years... well, doctor, it is actually quite perceptive of you to say two years specifically. Because that is exactly the timeframe we are looking at. This has all been going on since my close friend died a little over two years ago. I can pinpoint it almost to the exact week, to be perfectly honest with you. \n\nHer name was Helen, and we had known each other for... oh, it must have been going on thirty years. We started at the bank around the exact same time back in the eighties. She was over in the safety deposit boxes for a while before moving to the main teller line, and we just clicked immediately. We used to go to this little diner down the street for lunch every single Friday, rain or shine. They had a wonderful clam chowder, the creamy New England kind, not that red Manhattan nonsense. But then she got sick, and it just happened so incredibly fast. She passed away a little over two years ago, right in the early spring. \n\nAnd ever since then... well, to answer your question about whether the intensity has changed, I would have to say no. It really hasn't changed at all. It hasn't gotten worse, I suppose, but it certainly hasn't gotten any better, either. It just... descended on me. It is like a heavy, damp wool blanket that someone draped over my shoulders right after her funeral, and I just have not been able to shrug it off since. \n\nYou would think time would heal all wounds, as the old saying goes, or at least that the heaviness would ebb and flow. You know, maybe feel a little lighter on a beautiful sunny day, or when I'm balancing the books for the historical society like I mentioned before. But it doesn't. It is just this constant, steady, unrelenting flat feeling, day in and day out, ever since I lost her. I keep waiting for a morning where I wake up and it feels even just a fraction lighter, but it just stays exactly the same...\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight since you started feeling this way?\n\nPatient: Weight? Oh... no, no I haven't. You know, you hear about people wasting away when they go through a hard time, but that hasn't happened to me at all. \n\nI suppose it is because I am very rigidly tied to my routine. I wake up, I have my piece of toast and my tea at seven-thirty. Then at noon, I have my lunch. I used to go out to that diner with Helen, like I said, but now I just bring a simple turkey sandwich and eat it at my desk while I review the afternoon's loan applications. Just a small, simple thing, but I would think about it on Thursday and Friday, just anticipating it.\n\nBut now? I haven't been to Olsen's in... oh, goodness, it must be over a year. The thought of getting in the car, driving down there, finding parking on Main Street which is always a nightmare on weekends anyway, and then making small talk with Mrs. Olsen... she always asks about the kids, which is lovely of her, it really is, but it just takes so much energy to smile and give all the updates and pretend everything is just fine and dandy. It just feels so exhausting even thinking about it. So I stopped going. I just eat my plain oatmeal on Saturdays now, same as every other day.\n\nAnd you'd think maybe I'd look forward to the evenings, right? After being at the bank all day, dealing with people's credit scores and debt consolidations and all the endless paperwork—you'd think I'd be eager to just come home and take my shoes off. But coming home just means walking into an empty house where the quiet is just... well, it's almost deafening. So I don't look forward to that either. \n\nI just exist through the day, really. I wake up, I go to the bank, I come home, I go to sleep. I can't really pinpoint a single thing, big or small, that gives me that little flutter of anticipation anymore. It's just a long stretch of gray, if that makes sense. Just... flat.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities, no matter how small, that you still find yourself looking forward to?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying with the bakery... I really wish I could give you a different answer, I truly do. Because it sounds so awful to sit here and say no, doesn't it? But... no. There really isn't anything at all. \n\nI try to think about my work, you know, because being a loan officer, you get to be part of these big moments in people's lives. I used to look forward to closing days so much. Oh, closing days were just wonderful. I’d have this special folder I’d put their paperwork in—a nice, heavy cardstock one, a deep burgundy color, not those flimsy cheap manila ones the bank orders in bulk. I’d buy them myself at the office supply store just for my first-time homebuyers. I'd look forward to seeing their faces light up when everything was finalized, knowing I helped them get their starter home. \n\nBut now? I see a closing on my calendar and I just feel... tired. It’s just more signatures to witness, more copies to make, more files to scan into the system. It doesn't matter if it's a big thing like a closing day, or a tiny thing like... well, like watching Jeopardy. I used to watch Jeopardy every single night at 7:00 PM sharp. I'd rush through doing the dinner dishes just to make sure I was sitting in my armchair before the music started. The noise of it just feels grating, somehow, so I just sit in the quiet. \n\nSo, I search and search my mind, doctor, because I want to be helpful, I want to say 'yes, this one little thing gives me something to look forward to,' but I'd just be making it up. I don't... I don't find pleasure in them anymore. Any of them, really. \n\nTake my garden, for instance. I mentioned my flower beds earlier. I have these wonderful hydrangeas along the south side of the house—they've been there for years, and I always took such meticulous care of them. I used to get so much joy out of tinkering with the soil acidity, you know, adding just the right amount of aluminum sulfate so the blooms would turn this brilliant, deep blue instead of pink. I’d spend hours out there on my weekends, and when a neighbor would walk by and compliment them, I’d just beam. I felt so much pride and genuine happiness just getting my hands dirty. \n\nBut now? I still go out there, because if I don't, the weeds will take over and the bushes will look terrible, and I can't stand the thought of the neighbors whispering about the state of my yard. So I drag myself out there, I kneel down on my little green foam pad, I take my pruning shears, and I clip away the dead blooms. But while I'm doing it, I just feel... empty.
